title: To act, we must be confident we can make an impact and feel what we do is important
why: To act at all, we need some belief that our choices matter and that we can pull them off. A bit of extra confidence gets us moving, keeps us going after setbacks, and protects our sense of self-worth and our standing in a group.
cost: We misjudge our own skills, blame others unfairly, and take risks we don't see. We also misread how much others share our views or how easily they are swayed.
spot: You feel sure of an answer but could not say how you would check it.
You are forming a strong opinion of someone from a single moment or incident.
You feel like the rules and odds that apply to other people don't quite apply to you.
fix: Before a big decision, write down how sure you are and review it later against what actually happened.
Ask someone who disagrees with you to name the weakest part of your plan.
Invite regular feedback from people who have nothing to gain by flattering you.

biases.d: Our confidence in our own judgments is often higher than our actual accuracy. We feel more certain than our track record justifies.
biases.ex: A manager is certain a project will ship in three months because the plan looks solid, and it takes seven.
biases.q: You take a trivia quiz and mark every answer as 'definitely right,' but when the scores come back you got only about half of them.
biases.spot: Ask yourself how often you have felt this sure before and still turned out to be wrong.
biases.fix: Give a range instead of a single number, and make it wide enough that you'd be surprised if the answer fell outside it.

biases.d: The tendency to present ourselves in a flattering light, over-reporting good behavior and under-reporting bad behavior. It shows up strongly in surveys, interviews and other self-reports.
biases.ex: On a health survey, people report eating more vegetables and drinking less alcohol than they really do.
biases.q: Your doctor asks how many days a week you exercise, and you say 'four or so,' even though it has been one day most weeks lately.
biases.spot: Ask whether your answer would change if nobody could ever link it back to you.
biases.fix: When you need honest answers from others, use anonymous forms and neutral wording so no answer sounds like the 'right' one.

biases.d: The belief that media messages, ads and propaganda influence other people more than they influence us.
biases.ex: A man says political ads are brainwashing his neighbors while insisting the same ads have no effect on his own vote.
biases.q: After a documentary about social media manipulation, you worry about how much your teenage nephew is being shaped by his feed, while feeling sure your own habits are untouched.
biases.spot: Watch for the thought 'other people are so easily swayed by this' and ask why you would be the exception.
biases.fix: Trace one concrete choice, like a recent purchase or opinion, back to where you first heard about it.

biases.d: The tendency to overestimate how many people share our opinions, habits and values. We assume our own view is the normal one.
biases.ex: A voter is shocked when their candidate loses, because everyone they talked to planned to vote the same way.
biases.q: You book a team lunch at a very spicy Thai place, sure that basically everyone loves heat as much as you do, and are surprised when half the team asks for something else.
biases.spot: Ask yourself whether you actually know what others think, or whether you are filling the gap with your own view.
biases.fix: Before assuming agreement, ask a few people directly, including some outside your usual circle.

biases.d: The tendency to be overconfident on hard tasks and underconfident on easy ones. Our sense of how well we did does not adjust enough to how difficult the task really was.
biases.ex: A student feels good about a brutal calculus exam and scores poorly, then worries about a simple quiz and aces it.
biases.q: You feel sure you nailed a tough job interview full of technical puzzles, yet you fret over a short, simple phone screen, and the results come back the other way around.
biases.spot: Notice whether your gut feeling about a result stays about the same no matter how demanding the task was.
biases.fix: On hard tasks, lower your confidence a notch on purpose, and on easy ones, give yourself more credit.

biases.d: The tendency for most members of a group to rate themselves as above the group's average, which cannot be true for everyone. It is named after a fictional town where 'all the children are above average,' and is another name for illusory superiority.
biases.ex: At a company, nearly every salesperson believes their customer service is better than the team's average.
biases.q: At a parents' evening, you notice that every parent you talk to describes their own child as ahead of most of the class.
biases.spot: When you rank yourself against a group, ask whether most of the others would rank themselves the same way.
biases.fix: In group reviews, rank people against each other using real data, since everyone cannot sit above the middle.

biases.d: People with little skill in an area tend to overrate their ability, partly because spotting mistakes takes the same know-how as avoiding them, while experts sometimes underrate themselves. Researchers still debate how large the effect is.
biases.ex: After a week of lessons, a beginner chess player feels ready to beat club players, while a veteran talks mostly about how much she still doesn't know.
biases.q: After fixing one leaky faucet with the help of a video, you tell your family you can rewire the kitchen yourself, while the electrician next door says even she double-checks every job.
biases.spot: Ask yourself how much you actually know about what experts in this area worry about.
biases.fix: Get feedback from someone skilled before you judge your own work, and ask them what beginners usually miss.

biases.d: The tendency to rely too much on our own point of view, including remembering our own part in shared events as bigger or better than it was.
biases.ex: Two roommates each believe they do about two-thirds of the housework, which adds up to more than the whole.
biases.q: After a group project, you tell your partner you did most of the hard work, then learn that each of your three teammates privately claimed the same.
biases.spot: Notice when your account of a shared effort features you far more than anyone else.
biases.fix: Before claiming credit, list in detail what each other person did, as if you were writing their review.

biases.d: The tendency to believe we are less likely than other people to face bad events, like illness, accidents or divorce, and more likely to enjoy good ones.
biases.ex: A smoker agrees that smoking causes cancer but feels sure it won't happen to them.
biases.q: You skip travel insurance for a ski trip because injuries happen to other skiers, even though you ski the same slopes they do.
biases.spot: Ask yourself what actually makes you different from the typical person this bad outcome happens to.
biases.fix: Look up how often the bad outcome happens to people like you and plan as if that rate applied to you.

biases.d: The tendency to rate vague, general personality descriptions as highly accurate for us personally. It is named after psychologist Bertram Forer, who showed it using a personality test, and is another name for the Barnum effect.
biases.ex: Everyone in a workshop gets the 'personalized' results of a personality quiz, and most rate theirs as a great fit, unaware that all the reports say the same thing.
biases.q: A career coach hands you a 'custom' profile saying you value security but crave change, and you are amazed at how well it captures you, until a friend shows you the identical profile.
biases.spot: Ask whether the description would fit your friends just as well as it fits you.
biases.fix: Swap your results with someone else's and see whether theirs fits you just as well.

biases.d: Another name for the Forer effect: we accept vague statements that could apply to almost anyone as a precise description of ourselves. It is named after showman P.T. Barnum and the idea of offering 'something for everyone.'
biases.ex: A horoscope says 'you have hidden potential that others haven't noticed yet,' and many readers feel it was written just for them.
biases.q: A palm reader at a street fair tells you that you sometimes doubt your choices and have a creative side you rarely show, and you leave convinced she has a real gift.
biases.spot: Notice when a statement feels deeply true about you but leans on words like 'sometimes,' 'at times' or 'deep down.'
biases.fix: Write down what a reading or quiz says, then check whether it made any claim specific enough to be proven wrong.

biases.d: The habit of taking credit for our successes while blaming outside factors for our failures. It protects our self-esteem.
biases.ex: A student who aces a test credits her hard work, but after failing the next one she blames the unfair questions.
biases.q: When your team wins a pitch, you point to your slide design, and when the next pitch fails, you say the client never had the budget anyway.
biases.spot: Compare how you explain your wins with how you explain your losses, and check whether the causes switch sides.
biases.fix: After any result, name one thing you did and one outside factor that contributed, whether it went well or badly.

biases.d: The tendency to explain our own actions by the situation but other people's actions by their character. It is closely related to the fundamental attribution error.
biases.ex: When you snap at a cashier, it's because you had a terrible day, but when a cashier snaps at you, they're just rude.
biases.q: You arrive late to a meeting and explain that traffic was awful, but when a coworker arrives late the next day, you decide he's just disorganized.
biases.spot: Notice when you excuse yourself with circumstances but judge someone else with a label.
biases.fix: When you judge someone, ask what explanation you would give if you had done the exact same thing.

biases.d: The tendency to believe we can influence outcomes that are really out of our hands, such as chance events.
biases.ex: Some dice players throw harder when they want high numbers and more gently when they want low ones.
biases.q: You insist on choosing your own lottery numbers instead of a random pick, because you feel numbers you chose give you a better shot.
biases.spot: Ask yourself whether your action can actually change the outcome, or just makes you feel involved.
biases.fix: Separate what you can influence from what is pure chance, and put your effort only into the first list.

biases.d: The tendency to overestimate our own qualities and abilities compared with other people. The Lake Wobegone effect is another name for it.
biases.ex: Most drivers believe they are safer and more skilled than the typical driver on the road.
biases.q: You think of yourself as a better listener, kinder and more honest than most of your friends, though you've never asked any of them how they see it.
biases.spot: Watch for the thought 'I'm not like most people' when it comes to a skill or a virtue.
biases.fix: Pick one skill you rate highly and test it against an objective benchmark, like a timed test or a recording of yourself.

biases.d: The tendency to explain other people's behavior by their personality while underrating the situation they are in.
biases.ex: A driver who cuts you off gets labeled a jerk, though they might be rushing someone to the hospital.
biases.q: A new waiter forgets your order twice, and you decide he's lazy and careless, without knowing he's covering eight tables alone on his first shift.
biases.spot: Notice when you jump from one action to a firm judgment about who someone is.
biases.fix: Before judging, list at least two outside pressures that could make a decent person act this way.

biases.d: The tendency to assign blame in ways that protect us from feeling we could suffer, or cause, the same harm. We blame the person responsible more as the outcome gets more severe, and we blame a victim less when they seem similar to us.
biases.ex: When a house burns down from a forgotten candle, a person who often lights candles calls it bad luck, while someone who never does calls the owner careless.
biases.q: When a neighbor's small kitchen fire is put out quickly, you call it an accident, but when an identical mistake burns down a whole building, you insist the person must have been reckless.
biases.spot: Notice when your blame grows with how bad the outcome was, even though the actions were the same.
biases.fix: Judge a choice by what the person knew at the time, then note separately how bad the result turned out.

biases.d: The tendency to see ourselves as flexible and changeable in personality, mood and behavior, while seeing other people as fixed and predictable.
biases.ex: A person says their own moods depend on the day but describes a coworker as 'always negative.'
biases.q: Asked to describe yourself, you say 'it depends on the situation,' but you sum up your sister in three firm words: stubborn, loud and cheerful.
biases.spot: Notice when you describe others with fixed labels but describe yourself with 'it depends.'
biases.fix: When you label someone, recall a specific time they acted against that label.

biases.d: The tendency to value an outcome more because we worked hard or suffered to get it. It eases the discomfort of thinking the effort might have been wasted.
biases.ex: Members of a club with a harsh initiation often rate the club more highly than members who joined easily.
biases.q: After waiting four hours in line for a restaurant's famous burger, you rave that it's the best you've ever eaten, while a friend who walked in with no wait found it ordinary.
biases.spot: Ask whether you would value the result as much if it had been handed to you for free.
biases.fix: Judge the outcome by comparing it with alternatives, and leave the effort you spent out of the scoring.

biases.d: The tendency to take more risks when we feel safer and to act more carefully when we feel more at risk. Safety measures can lose part of their benefit this way.
biases.ex: A cyclist wearing a new helmet rides faster through traffic than they would without it.
biases.q: After buying a car with automatic emergency braking, you start checking your phone at red lights and following the car ahead more closely.
biases.spot: Notice when new safety gear or a backup plan makes you relax your other habits.
biases.fix: When you add a safety measure, decide in advance that your other careful habits stay exactly the same.

biases.d: Another name for risk compensation, often used for safety rules and regulations: when a law makes an activity safer, people may act less carefully and cancel out some of the gain. It is named after economist Sam Peltzman.
biases.ex: After a town adds guardrails to a winding road, some drivers start taking the curves faster than before.
biases.q: Once your company starts backing up every file automatically each hour, you and your coworkers stop saving copies of important work and delete drafts far more casually.
biases.spot: Ask whether a new rule that protects you has quietly changed how carefully you act.
biases.fix: When a new safety rule arrives, track the actual results over time, in addition to whether people follow the rule.

title: To stay focused, we favor the immediate, relatable thing in front of us
why: Attention and energy are limited, so the brain gives priority to what is here, now and personal. Things we can see clearly or picture in detail feel more real and urgent than distant or abstract ones. Reacting quickly to the reward or threat in front of us often mattered more than planning for a far-off future.
cost: We trade away bigger future rewards for small ones today, chase the new over the proven, and let one vivid story outweigh the needs of many people.
spot: The choice feels urgent, but the pressure is one you created yourself.
A single face, story or shiny feature is doing most of the persuading.
You are weighing how you feel today much more than how things will look next year.
fix: Picture your future self in detail, a year from now, living with the result of this choice.
Put the numbers and the single story side by side, and give each its fair weight.
Set a waiting period, such as 24 hours, before acting on something that feels exciting and fresh.

biases.d: The tendency to strongly prefer smaller rewards now over larger rewards later, with the pull of 'now' growing sharply as a reward gets close. It explains why we make sensible plans for the future and then abandon them when the moment arrives.
biases.ex: Offered $100 today or $110 next month, many people take the $100, yet they would happily wait the extra month if both choices were a year away.
biases.q: On Sunday you plan to skip dessert all week to reach your fitness goal, but on Tuesday night the cake in the fridge wins, and it wins again on Wednesday.
biases.spot: Notice when a plan you made for 'later' falls apart the moment 'later' becomes 'now.'
biases.fix: Lock in the future choice ahead of time, for example with automatic savings transfers or a pre-paid class.

biases.d: A reasoning error where we assume an idea, product or method is better simply because it is new. It is the mirror image of assuming the old way is best because it is traditional.
biases.ex: A company switches to the latest project-management app every year, assuming each one must be an improvement.
biases.q: You replace a phone that works perfectly with this year's model because the ad calls it the 'latest,' though you can't name one thing it would do better for you.
biases.spot: Ask yourself what the new option does better, apart from being new.
biases.fix: List the concrete benefits the new option offers over the current one, and switch only if the list holds up.

biases.d: The tendency to feel more for, and give more to, one specific person with a name and a face than a large group of unnamed people with the same need.
biases.ex: A news story about one trapped child draws huge donations, while a report about thousands of children in the same danger draws far fewer.
biases.q: A charity letter with a photo and the story of one girl named Amara moves you to donate, but the same charity's letter describing 20,000 families in need goes straight into the recycling.
biases.spot: Notice when a single face moves you more than a much larger number of people in the same situation.
biases.fix: When a single story moves you, look up how many people share that need and decide how to help the most of them.

title: To get things done, we tend to complete things we've invested time and energy in
why: Finishing what we start is usually a good strategy, since a brain that quit at every bump would never complete anything. Valuing what we already have, what we built and what we worked for keeps us committed and protects our resources. Losing what we have can hurt more than an equal gain helps, so caution around losses often makes sense.
cost: We keep pouring time, money and pride into things that no longer deserve it, and we overvalue what is ours while dismissing better options.
spot: Your main reason for continuing is how much you've already put in.
You would never pay today's price to get the thing you now refuse to give up.
Evidence against your choice makes you dig in harder instead of reconsidering.
fix: Ask what you would decide if you were starting fresh today, with nothing already invested.
Set stopping points in advance, such as a budget or a deadline, and stick to them.
Have someone with no stake in the outcome review whether to continue.

biases.d: The tendency to keep going with something because of the time, money or effort already spent, even when continuing costs more than it returns. Past costs cannot be recovered, so they shouldn't drive future choices.
biases.ex: You sit through a boring, expensive concert to the very end because the tickets cost so much.
biases.q: You're halfway through a 600-page novel you've disliked since chapter two, and you force yourself to finish because you've already spent so many evenings on it.
biases.spot: Ask whether you would start this today, knowing what you know now.
biases.fix: Decide based only on future costs and benefits, and treat what's already spent as gone either way.

biases.d: The tendency to keep raising our investment in a losing decision to justify what we've already put in, often in a competitive setting. It is closely related to escalation of commitment and the sunk cost fallacy.
biases.ex: In a bidding war, two buyers push the price of a house far above what either planned to pay, because neither wants their earlier bids to have been for nothing.
biases.q: In an online auction for a vintage guitar, you keep topping the other bidder long past your limit, because backing out now would mean all your earlier bids were wasted.
biases.spot: Notice when beating the other side has become the goal, more than the prize itself.
biases.fix: Write down your walk-away number before any bidding or negotiation starts, and give it to someone who will hold you to it.

biases.d: A pattern where people or organizations keep backing a failing course of action because they've already committed to it, often to avoid admitting a mistake. It is closely related to irrational escalation and the sunk cost fallacy.
biases.ex: A government keeps funding a delayed, over-budget building project because stopping would mean admitting the earlier spending was a mistake.
biases.q: Your company's software rollout has missed three deadlines and users hate it, yet you, the manager who proposed it, ask for another year of funding instead of pulling the plug.
biases.spot: Ask whether your reluctance to stop is about the project's future or about protecting your earlier decision.
biases.fix: Have someone who wasn't part of the original decision review whether the effort should continue.

biases.d: A memory effect: we remember information better when we produce it ourselves than when we simply read or hear it. It helps learning, and it also makes our own ideas feel more familiar and valuable than they may be.
biases.ex: A student who fills in the blanks on flashcards remembers more than one who just rereads the complete answers.
biases.q: Studying for a test, you cover the answers and try to produce them from memory, and those facts stick far better than the ones you only read through.
biases.spot: Notice when an idea seems stronger to you mainly because you came up with it.
biases.fix: This effect can work for you: when learning, quiz yourself or explain ideas in your own words instead of rereading them.

biases.d: The tendency to feel the pain of losing something more strongly than the pleasure of gaining something of equal value. Losing $50 usually feels worse than finding $50 feels good.
biases.ex: Shoppers are often more motivated by 'avoid a $5 fee' than by 'get a $5 discount,' though the money is the same.
biases.q: You turn down a coin-flip bet that would pay you $120 on heads and cost you $100 on tails, because the thought of the $100 gone outweighs the bigger prize.
biases.spot: Ask whether you are rejecting a good deal just because it includes a chance of giving something up.
biases.fix: Frame the choice both ways, once as a gain and once as a loss, and see whether your answer changes.

biases.d: The tendency to value things more highly when we have helped build or create them, even when the result is imperfect. It is named after the furniture store whose products buyers assemble themselves.
biases.ex: A person values their wobbly homemade bookshelf more than a sturdier store-bought one.
biases.q: At a cooking class, you rate the pasta you made yourself as better than the chef's, even though your sauce is clearly lumpy.
biases.spot: Ask whether you would rate this as highly if someone else had made it.
biases.fix: Have someone who didn't help make it judge the quality before you decide how good it is.

biases.d: The tendency to treat one serving, portion or item as the right amount to finish, whatever its size. We tend to complete whatever single package is in front of us.
biases.ex: People eat more popcorn from a large bucket than from a medium one, because they keep eating until the container is empty.
biases.q: At the movies you finish an entire jumbo bag of candy, though a snack-size pack would have satisfied you just as much.
biases.spot: Notice when you stop because the container is empty and not because you've had enough.
biases.fix: Serve yourself smaller portions, or split large items before you start.

biases.d: The tendency to prefer completely removing a small risk over making a larger cut to a bigger risk. Eliminating a danger feels better than shrinking one, even when shrinking helps more.
biases.ex: Voters back a costly plan to wipe out a rare water contaminant over a cheaper plan that would halve a much more common health threat.
biases.q: Choosing between two home upgrades, you pay for the one that fully removes a tiny chance of a minor pipe leak instead of the one that would greatly cut the much likelier chance of a basement flood.
biases.spot: Ask whether you're choosing the option that feels completely safe instead of the one that prevents the most harm.
biases.fix: Compare options by the total amount of harm each one prevents.

biases.d: The tendency to sell things that have risen in value too early and to hold on to things that have fallen in value too long, hoping to get back to even.
biases.ex: An investor sells a stock after a small gain to lock it in, but keeps one that has dropped 40 percent because selling would make the loss feel 'real.'
biases.q: You quickly resell the concert tickets whose resale price went up, but hang on to the ones whose price dropped, waiting for them to climb back to what you paid.
biases.spot: Notice when your decision to sell depends on the price you paid, which has no bearing on what happens next.
biases.fix: For each thing you hold, ask whether you would buy it today at today's price, and act on that answer.

biases.d: The tendency to treat an outcome as certain when it is only certain within one stage of a multi-stage situation. We overvalue options that remove risk at one step, even when the overall result is still uncertain.
biases.ex: A contest promises that anyone who reaches the final round wins a prize, and entrants plan around the prize as a sure thing, though most never reach the final.
biases.q: Your contract promises a guaranteed bonus if the company hits its yearly target, and you book a vacation with the money as though it were already paid, even though hitting the target is far from assured.
biases.spot: Ask whether the guarantee you're counting on depends on an earlier step that could still fail.
biases.fix: Work out the odds of every stage together to find the true overall chance before you decide.

biases.d: A memory effect: information that takes more effort to read or understand tends to be remembered better, because we think about it more deeply. It helps learning, though it can also make hard-won details stick even when they aren't the most important.
biases.ex: Students often remember a tricky, dense paragraph from a textbook better than the easy summary printed next to it.
biases.q: You breeze through a light news article and forget it by lunch, but a hard-to-read legal letter you puzzled over for twenty minutes stays with you for weeks.
biases.spot: Notice whether the ideas you remember best are the important ones or just the ones that were hardest to follow.
biases.fix: This effect can work for you: when studying, work through material actively, by rewriting it or solving problems, instead of skimming an easy version.

biases.d: The tendency to value something more just because we own it. People often ask much more to give up an item than they would pay to buy it.
biases.ex: Someone given a free coffee mug asks far more to sell it than they would have paid for the same mug in a shop.
biases.q: You list your used couch for far more than you'd ever pay for a similar used couch, and you feel insulted when buyers offer the going rate.
biases.spot: Ask what you would pay for this item if you didn't already own it.
biases.fix: Check what similar items actually sell for, and use that as your price.

biases.d: The tendency for some people, when shown evidence against a belief they hold dearly, to hold that belief even more strongly. Later research suggests it is less common than first thought, but it can happen when a belief is tied to identity.
biases.ex: After a friend shares an article that disproves a health myth, the believer starts sharing the myth even more often.
biases.q: When your uncle shows you a fact check proving your favorite claim about a politician is false, you leave the conversation more convinced than ever that the claim is true.
biases.spot: Notice when strong evidence against your view makes you angrier and more certain instead of curious.
biases.fix: Decide in advance what specific evidence would change your mind, and hold yourself to it.

title: To avoid mistakes, we aim to preserve autonomy and group status, and avoid irreversible decisions
why: Keeping our freedom to choose and our standing in a group protects us from being exploited or pushed out. Sticking with what already works, and avoiding choices we can't undo, limits the damage of a bad call. These habits likely helped people get by in small groups, where losing status or making a costly mistake could be serious.
cost: We defend flawed systems, do the opposite of good advice just to feel free, and let comparisons and clever framing steer our choices.
spot: You feel a flash of irritation the moment someone tells you what to do.
The main appeal of an option is that it keeps things as they are.
Your choice is shaped more by how an option compares with others nearby than by what you need.
fix: Write down what you actually need before looking at the options on offer.
Separate the advice from the person giving it, and judge the advice on its merits.
Treat 'keep things as they are' as one option among several, with its own costs.

biases.d: The tendency to defend and justify the existing social, economic or political order, even when it works against our own interests. It makes the current system feel fair and natural.
biases.ex: Employees at a company with an unfair promotion system insist it rewards merit, even as they watch it pass them over.
biases.q: Your school's grading policy clearly penalizes students who work jobs after class, including you, yet you argue the policy is fair and anyone who complains is just making excuses.
biases.spot: Ask whether you're defending a rule because it's fair or because it's familiar and already in place.
biases.fix: Imagine designing the system from scratch without knowing which role you'd end up in, and compare it with the current one.

biases.d: A persuasion tactic where someone argues for the opposite of what they want, counting on the other person to push back and do the desired thing. It works by triggering reactance, and it steers us most when we don't notice it.
biases.ex: A parent tells a picky child 'you probably wouldn't like broccoli anyway,' and the child insists on trying it.
biases.q: A car salesperson says, 'Honestly, this model might be too much car for you,' and you find yourself arguing for why you should get it.
biases.spot: Notice when someone seems to be steering you away from something in a way that makes you want it more.
biases.fix: When someone tells you not to do something, ask what they would gain if you did it anyway.

biases.d: The urge to do the opposite of what someone wants when we feel our freedom to choose is being threatened. The harder the push, the stronger the pushback.
biases.ex: A teenager told to stop seeing a friend starts spending even more time with that friend.
biases.q: A sign in the park says 'Keep off the grass, no exceptions,' and you suddenly feel an urge to cut across the lawn, though you never wanted to before.
biases.spot: Ask whether you want this thing for itself or because someone said you can't have it.
biases.fix: Restate the request in your own words as a choice you're free to make, then decide on the merits.

biases.d: The tendency for our choice between two options to change when a third, clearly inferior option is added. The added option makes one of the original two look better by comparison.
biases.ex: A cinema sells small popcorn for $4 and large for $8, then adds a medium for $7.50, and suddenly most people buy the large.
biases.q: You were going to buy the cheaper of two blenders until the store placed a third one beside the pricier model, costing almost as much but with fewer features, and now the pricier one looks like a steal.
biases.spot: Ask whether you would still choose the same option if the least attractive choice on the menu disappeared.
biases.fix: Remove any option you would never pick, then compare the remaining ones directly.

biases.d: The tendency to feel dislike or competitiveness toward people who seem better than us in some way, which can lead us to hold them back. It often shows up in hiring and promotion decisions.
biases.ex: A manager passes on a brilliant job candidate who might outshine her and picks someone less threatening instead.
biases.q: When a talented new colleague joins your team, you find yourself pointing out her small errors in meetings and quietly leaving her off a big project you lead.
biases.spot: Notice when someone's strengths make you want to hunt for their flaws.
biases.fix: Use a written list of criteria when judging others, and ask a neutral colleague to score them too.

biases.d: The preference for keeping things as they are, even when a change would be better. The current state becomes the reference point, and any change feels like a risk.
biases.ex: Many people stay with a default pension plan or phone contract for years without comparing better options.
biases.q: Your internet bill has crept up every year and a rival offers faster service for less, but you stay with your current provider because switching feels like a bother, even though it takes one phone call.
biases.spot: Ask whether you would choose your current situation if you were picking fresh today.
biases.fix: Once a year, review your defaults, such as plans, subscriptions and routines, as if you were signing up for the first time.

title: We favor simple-looking options and complete information over complex, ambiguous options
why: Simple, clear options are faster to understand and easier to act on, and when time is short that speed matters. Known odds and complete information feel safer because they let us predict what will happen. Preferring the clear option often saves effort that would be wasted on puzzles we can't solve.
cost: We avoid good options just because they are uncertain, chase details that won't change our decision, and trust arguments for their neatness instead of their logic.
spot: You're spending most of your time on the easiest part of a problem while the hardest part waits.
A statement feels true mainly because it sounds neat, catchy or tidy.
You keep asking for more data even though you already know what you'd do.
fix: Decide how much time a choice deserves based on its stakes, and stop researching when you reach that limit.
When an argument feels satisfying, check its steps one by one before accepting it.
When an option looks clean and simple, ask what complexity it might be hiding.

biases.d: The tendency to avoid options where the odds of a good outcome are unknown and to pick options with known odds instead, even when the unknown option might be better.
biases.ex: Given a jar with exactly half red balls and a jar with an unknown mix, most people choose to draw from the known jar, though the other could be just as good.
biases.q: At a carnival you choose the game whose sign says '1 in 4 wins' over the one with no posted odds, though you have no reason to think the second is any worse.
biases.spot: Notice when missing information is the only reason you're rejecting an option.
biases.fix: Estimate a rough range for the unknown odds and compare that range with the known option.

biases.d: The tendency to seek more information even when it cannot change what we will do. Extra data can feel like progress while only delaying the decision.
biases.ex: A doctor orders extra tests that would not change the treatment plan, just to feel more thorough.
biases.q: You've already decided to buy the laptop that fits your budget, but you spend three more evenings reading reviews of models you would never buy.
biases.spot: Ask what you would do differently if this new piece of information came back one way or the other.
biases.fix: Set a deadline for research, and when it arrives, decide with what you have.

biases.d: The tendency to judge an argument by whether we agree with its conclusion instead of by whether its reasoning holds up. A weak argument seems strong if we like where it lands.
biases.ex: People accept 'All flowers need water; roses need water; so roses are flowers' as logical because the conclusion is true, though the reasoning is broken.
biases.q: In a debate, you rate the side that reaches the conclusion you already hold as 'more logical,' though a teacher later shows its reasoning had a clear gap and the other side's did not.
biases.spot: Ask whether you would accept the same reasoning if it led to a conclusion you dislike.
biases.fix: Test an argument's logic by swapping in a conclusion you disagree with and checking whether the steps still work.

biases.d: The tendency to judge a statement as more accurate or true when it rhymes. The sound makes it easier to process, and that ease feels like truth.
biases.ex: 'Woes unite foes' can sound wiser than 'Woes unite enemies,' though the meaning is the same.
biases.q: A diet ad's slogan, 'Snack smart, save your heart,' convinces you more than the same advice from your doctor phrased as 'Choose healthier snacks for better heart health.'
biases.spot: Notice when a catchy, sing-song phrase is doing most of the persuading.
biases.fix: Reword the claim in plain language and judge whether it still holds up.

biases.d: The tendency for groups to spend lots of time on small, easy-to-grasp details while rushing through complex, important ones. It is another name for the law of triviality, from an example of a committee that argues about a bike shed and quickly approves a nuclear plant.
biases.ex: A software team argues for an hour about button colors and approves the database design in five minutes.
biases.q: Your neighborhood association spends the whole meeting debating what color to paint the mailboxes and approves the major road repair contract in the last two minutes.
biases.spot: Notice when the group is debating something everyone feels qualified to weigh in on while the hard item sits untouched.
biases.fix: Set a strict time limit for small decisions and let one person make the call.

biases.d: An observation by C. Northcote Parkinson that groups give too much time to trivial issues and too little to big, complex ones, so the time spent on an item can shrink as its cost grows. It is another name for the bike-shedding effect.
biases.ex: A city council spends most of a session on the wording of a park bench plaque and passes the annual budget with little discussion.
biases.q: In your department's budget review, a multi-million-dollar software contract passes with barely a question, while the $200 line for team snacks sparks a forty-minute argument.
biases.spot: Compare how long a discussion runs with how much money or risk is actually at stake.
biases.fix: Put the costliest item first on the agenda, while people are fresh and focused.

biases.d: The tendency to set clear, detailed goals for less important tasks while leaving our most important goals vague. Big goals are hard and uncomfortable to define, so we busy ourselves with the easy ones.
biases.ex: Someone has a precise weekly plan for reorganizing their closet but only a fuzzy idea of 'someday changing careers.'
biases.q: Your to-do list has step-by-step instructions for planning a friend's birthday dinner, but your top life priority, 'get healthier,' has no plan, date or first step.
biases.spot: Ask whether your most important goal is written down as specifically as your smallest ones.
biases.fix: Break your biggest goal into one concrete next step with a date on it.

biases.d: The mistake of judging a specific combination of events as more likely than one of those events alone. Adding details makes a story feel more believable while making it less likely.
biases.ex: Told about a woman who cares deeply about social justice, many people rate 'bank teller and feminist' as more likely than just 'bank teller,' which is impossible.
biases.q: Told your new neighbor is quiet and loves books, you think it's more likely he's 'a librarian who writes poetry' than simply 'a librarian.'
biases.spot: Notice when adding details to a story makes it feel more likely.
biases.fix: Check each added detail and remember that every 'and' can only lower the odds.

biases.d: A problem-solving principle that says, among competing explanations, the one with the fewest assumptions should usually be preferred. It is a useful rule of thumb, but as a bias it leads us to favor a simple explanation even when the evidence points to a more complex one.
biases.ex: A company blames falling sales on one new competitor and ignores several smaller causes that together explain the drop better.
biases.q: Your houseplant is wilting and you decide it just needs more water, ignoring that it also sits in a cold draft and its roots have outgrown the pot.
biases.spot: Ask whether your explanation accounts for all the facts, or only the ones that fit neatly.
biases.fix: List every fact that needs explaining and check that your chosen explanation covers each one.

biases.d: A preference reversal where a smaller or cheaper option is preferred when judged on its own, while the larger or better option wins when the two are compared side by side. Without a comparison, we judge by easy cues like how full or complete something looks.
biases.ex: Seen separately, an overfilled small cup of ice cream seems more generous than a larger amount in a half-empty big cup.
biases.q: Browsing separate listings, you'd pay more for a 20-piece dish set in perfect shape than for a 40-piece set with a few chipped plates, even though the larger set still has more intact pieces.
biases.spot: Ask whether your judgment would change if you saw both options next to each other.
biases.fix: Compare options side by side, using the same measures, before deciding.
